traits.notes: The seedling exhibits bipinnate or tripinnate compound leaves with sharply serrated leaflets. The overall appearance is consistent with certain palm species (such as *Licuala*), which often display this type of pinnate leaf architecture in their juvenile stages.

data.raw_response:
=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (leaves are grouped closely together at the tips of the stems)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (the leaf is divided into multiple distinct leaflets along a central axis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (there is a single terminal leaflet at the apex of the rachis)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 16 (estimated based on multiple views showing approximately 8 leaflet pairs plus a terminal leaflet)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): alternate (leaflets are attached at different points along the rachis, not in perfect pairs)
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.): toothed, serrate (margins have sharp, saw-like teeth pointing forward)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): lanceolate (leaflets are long and narrow, widest near the base and tapering to the tip)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acuminate (leaflets taper to a slender, pointed tip)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (leaflets are wedge-shaped, narrowing towards the attachment point)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (secondary veins branch off from a central midrib)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, pinnate arrangement with veins extending towards the margin
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (leaves reflect light, indicating a smooth, glossy surface)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no hairs are visible on the leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): long (the petiole is a distinct, elongated stalk connecting the leaf blade to the stem)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (the petiole appears cylindrical and round in cross-section)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): unclear (the main stem base is not clearly visible to determine if it is woody or herbaceous)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no hairs are visible on the visible parts of the stem)
    19. Stem color: green (the visible stems and rachises are green)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (the stem surface appears uniform and lacks prominent ridges or lenticels)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules are visible at the leaf bases)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joint-like structure is visible at the leaf base)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils are observed)
F. Notes: The seedling exhibits bipinnate or tripinnate compound leaves with sharply serrated leaflets. The overall appearance is consistent with certain palm species (such as *Licuala*), which often display this type of pinnate leaf architecture in their juvenile stages.
